summary: Defines a DHCPv6 option that tells a client using the EAP Re-authentication Protocol the name of its local domain. The client needs that name to derive domain-specific keys from the key material of an earlier authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: To get a visitor badge for a new building, you must know the building's name. This lets the network tell your device the name so it can quickly sign in again.

questions: erp local domain name dhcpv6 option
what is a domain specific root key
what is the erp local domain name option
how does a client learn the erp local domain name
subtitle: A DHCPv6 option that tells a device the local domain name it needs for fast EAP re-authentication.

tldr.problem: A device using the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP) needs the name of its local domain to derive a domain-specific root key, but no lower-layer way to learn that name had been defined.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the DHCPv6 option OPTION_ERP_LOCAL_DOMAIN_NAME (65), which carries the domain name as a DNS-encoded name. A client asks for it with an Option Request option, and a relay agent may supply it.
tldr.outcome: A DHCPv6 client can learn the ERP local domain name after full EAP authentication. The option is meant only for ERP, and it needs server authentication and integrity protection.

today: RFC 6440 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the DHCPv6 option for the ERP local domain name.

sections.title: Why ERP Needs a Domain Name
sections.content:
The EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP, RFC 5296) allows faster re-authentication of a mobile device that was earlier authenticated with the Extensible Authentication Protocol (RFC 3748). The local root key, for example a Domain-Specific Root Key (DSRK, RFC 5295), is generated using the local domain name (LDN). So the device must discover the LDN.

RFC 5296 says the LDN can be learned through the ERP exchange or by a lower-layer mechanism, but no lower-layer mechanism had yet been defined. RFC 6440 adds an extension to DHCPv6 for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: To get a quick re-entry pass, your device must know the name of the place it is in. This RFC gives the network a way to tell it.

sections.title: The ERP Local Domain Name Option
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 client uses the option to get the LDN from the DHCPv6 server after full EAP authentication has taken place. The contents are intended only for use with ERP and do not name a local domain for any other purpose.

The option has three parts: the option code OPTION_ERP_LOCAL_DOMAIN_NAME (65), option-length (the length of the name field, in octets), and erp-local-domain-name. The name MUST be encoded as in Section 8 of RFC 3315. That encoding allows internationalized domain names, but only as a set of A-labels (RFC 5890).
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small label with a number, a length, and then the name written in a standard way.

sections.title: Client and Relay Agent Behavior
sections.content:
A DHCPv6 client that does not know the ERP LDN and needs the server to provide it MUST include an Option Request option asking for the ERP Local Domain Name option (Section 22.7 of RFC 3315).

When the client receives the option with an LDN in it, it MUST check that the option length is no more than 256 octets, the maximum length of a single fully qualified domain name (FQDN) allowed by the DNS. It also MUST check that the name is a properly encoded single FQDN.

A DHCPv6 relay agent that already knows the ERP LDN for a client, for example from a previous AAA exchange, SHOULD include it in the option and forward it to the server as a suboption of the Relay-Supplied Options option (RFC 6422).
sections.plainLanguage: The device asks 'what is this place called?'. It checks that the answer is a proper name and not too long. A helper in the middle may already know it and pass it along.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The exchange of local domain name information between the DHCPv6 client and server is security sensitive. It requires server authentication and integrity protection. The RFC says the DHCPv6 security described in RFC 3315 can be used for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone gave your device a fake building name, it could get the wrong badge. So the device should be sure the answer comes from the real network and was not changed on the way.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content: IANA added the name OPTION_ERP_LOCAL_DOMAIN_NAME to the registry titled "Options Permitted in the Relay-Supplied Options Option". It also assigned one new option code in the "DHCP Option Codes" registry, referencing this document. The option format section gives that code as 65.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of option numbers got a new line, so everyone uses the same number for this option.
